problem_heading: Families Who Act in the First Week Win ICE Detention Cases

problem_cards.title: Find an ICE Detainee Before They're Transferred
problem_cards.body: Georgia and Florida hold some of the country's largest ICE facilities, and detainees are moved constantly — between Southeast facilities and into Georgia and Florida from across the country, often within days and without notice. Every transfer can mean a new court, a longer drive, and lost time. Locating your loved one and getting a lawyer on record (Form G-28) before the next transfer is the single most time-sensitive move a family can make. Immigration law is federal — we represent detainees in every state, by video or in person.

problem_cards.title: Immigration Bond Is Won With Evidence, Not a Plea
problem_cards.body: The judge weighs family ties, a stable address, work history, community roots, any record, and whether a sponsor will take responsibility. Families who show up with sponsor letters, proof of address, and documents win bonds; families who show up with only love and worry usually don't. We build that evidence package with you in days, so it's ready the moment the court is.

problem_cards.title: Don't Let Them Sign Anything in ICE Detention
problem_cards.body: Detained people are handed papers — stipulated removal orders, voluntary departure agreements — that can waive the right to ever see a judge. Signing to "get out faster" can mean leaving faster, permanently. The message to get to your loved one today, in any facility: sign nothing, and say you want to speak with a lawyer.

why_points.title: Built for the Family on the Outside
why_points.body: You're the one who can act. We work through you: you hire us — from anywhere in Texas or out of state — we get on record with the facility and the court, and we keep you informed at every step, in English or Spanish.

why_points.title: From Locating Them to Release, One Team
why_points.body: We find which Texas facility is holding them, enter appearance, request the bond hearing, build the release package, and stand next to them before the judge — then keep defending the removal case after they're out.

why_points.title: Straight Answers Under Pressure
why_points.body: Some detention is mandatory by law, and no honest lawyer pretends otherwise. We tell you within the first review whether bond is realistic for your loved one, what it will take, and what the alternatives are.

why_points.title: Flat Fees for Each Stage
why_points.body: The bond stage is quoted as one flat fee before we start. The removal defense that follows is quoted separately — so a family in crisis is never signing a blank check.

process.title: Step 1: Locate Them and Get on Record (G-28)
process.body: With a name, country of birth, and ideally the A-number, we find the facility — Texas has dozens, from Stewart and Folkston in Georgia to Krome, Broward Transitional, and Baker in Florida — file the G-28 attorney appearance, and make contact, usually within a business day.

process.title: Step 2: Build the Immigration Bond Case
process.body: We analyze eligibility (including whether any record triggers mandatory detention), identify the sponsor, and assemble the evidence: support letters, proof of address, family ties, employment, community roots.

process.title: Step 3: Win the Bond Hearing
process.body: We request the earliest possible hearing, present the package, prepare the sponsor and your loved one to answer the judge, and argue for release at the lowest realistic bond.

process.title: Step 4: Fight the Removal Case After Release
process.body: Release is the beginning, not the end — the removal case continues in immigration court. We screen every form of relief and keep defending, with your family member home while we fight.

fees_body: **To open the case: $2,500 down.** The retainer covers the first stage — locating your loved one, filing the G-28 to get on record, and preparing the bond request.
**How to pay:** credit or debit card. You do not need immigration status to hire us.

**Not included:** the bond itself, set by the judge (legal minimum $1,500, often higher). That is paid directly to ICE by someone with lawful status and refunded at the end of the case if your loved one attends every hearing.
**After bond:** the removal defense is quoted separately, stage by stage, flat fee. No blank checks.
**If the family can't put the retainer together today,** we'll say so respectfully: we can't open the case yet. Keep this page; when you're ready, call and we move the same day.

ui.faq_h2: ICE Detention & Immigration Bond Questions We Answer Every Week

faq.q: How do I find someone in ICE detention in Georgia or Florida?
faq.a: Use ICE's Online Detainee Locator (locator.ice.gov): search by A-number and country of birth, or by name, date of birth, and country. The A-number — 9 digits on any immigration paperwork — is the key, so look for old documents. Two Southeast realities: people booked in the last day or two may not appear yet, and detainees are transferred between facilities — and into Georgia and Florida from other states — without notice, so a location can go stale overnight. If you can't find them, that's exactly the first thing we do.

faq.q: Can my loved one get out on bond?
faq.a: Many detainees can — an immigration judge weighs family ties, a stable address, work history, community roots, and any record, and a strong sponsor package moves every one of those factors. But certain criminal history triggers mandatory detention with no bond, and people stopped at the border face a different process. We analyze which category applies in the first review and tell you straight.

faq.q: How much is immigration bond, and how is it paid?
faq.a: The legal minimum is $1,500; judges commonly set bonds in the several-thousand range or higher depending on the case. It's paid in full at an ICE bond office — and here's the detail families must plan for: the person who pays must show they're lawfully present in the U.S. If you don't have status yourself, line up a relative or friend who does. The money is refunded at the end of the case as long as your loved one attends every hearing.

faq.q: How fast can a bond hearing happen in Georgia or Florida?
faq.a: A bond request can be made at the first hearing or by written motion, and courts often schedule bond hearings within days to a few weeks — the wait varies by court, and the Stewart and Miami detained dockets move fast. What the family controls is readiness: the sponsor, the address proof, and the letters. When the package is ready the moment the court is, no time is wasted. That's why we start building it on day one.

faq.q: Should they sign anything ICE gives them?
faq.a: Not before a lawyer reads it. Stipulated removal orders and voluntary departure papers can waive the right to see a judge at all — people sign thinking it speeds up release and instead it speeds up removal. Everyone in detention has the right to say two things: "I do not want to sign" and "I want to speak with a lawyer." Get that message to your loved one through the facility phone as soon as you can.

faq.q: We don't live in Georgia or Florida — our loved one was transferred there. Can you still help?
faq.a: Yes. Immigration law is federal, so we can represent detainees held in Georgia and Florida facilities and appear in the courts that serve them regardless of where the family lives — many detained hearings are also conducted by video. Families work with us by phone, in English or Spanish, from anywhere. What we need from you is what you know: name, A-number if you have it, and where they were picked up.
